method: Read all 30 authoritativeHebrewLines of 2b (and raw 2a lines 35-39 for context only, and raw 3a line 1 to confirm the break) before reading currentDafSummary or any enrichment. Relevant Rashi used only as commentary. Every enrichment leaf of every sugya and the daf-level summary and glossary were then compared against the reconstruction.

independentSourceFlow.move: On 2a the Gemara answered that the milu'im verse links to the red heifer by 'tzivah'-'tzivah' (what here is separation, there too separation) and ended with 've-eima' (and say...). 2b physically starts by restating that challenge.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara (anonymous)
independentSourceFlow.move: Challenge: say instead the 'tzivah' of Yom Kippur, as written 'va-ya'as ka'asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe' (Lev 16:34).

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Answer: we derive a 'tzivah' that precedes the act from a 'tzivah' that precedes the act; we do not derive a 'tzivah' after the act from one before the act.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Challenge: say the 'tzivah' of the offerings, 'b'yom tzavoto et bnei Yisrael' (Lev 7:38). Answer: we derive 'tzivah' from 'tzivah', not 'tzavoto' from 'tzivah'. (Rashi: the proposal would require every kohen serving communal offerings to separate.)

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara, citing a baraita of the school of R. Yishmael
independentSourceFlow.move: Objection: what difference does it make? The school of R. Yishmael taught 've-shav ha-kohen', 'u-va ha-kohen' - this is returning, this is coming (two different verbs paired). (Rashi: as returning entails removing, scraping, plastering, so does coming.)

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Answer: that applies where there is nothing more similar; where there is something more similar, we learn from the more similar one.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Recalls 'le-chaper - these are the acts of Yom Kippur' and challenges: say the atonement of offerings (Rashi: individual offerings, 'and the kohen shall atone for him').

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Reply: do we know which kohen will be chosen (Rashi: by lot) who would need separation?

independentSourceFlow.speaker: 'amrei' (they say)
independentSourceFlow.move: Counter: why not? Let the entire beit av of the watch separate (Rashi: each family has its own day in the week).

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Answer: we derive a matter with a fixed time from a matter with a fixed time, excluding offerings which occur every day. (Rashi: the milu'im's fixed time, 1 Nisan, Ex 40.)

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Challenge: say the Festivals. Answer: we derive a matter practiced once a year from a matter practiced once a year, excluding Festivals which are not once a year.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Challenge: say one Festival; and if you object that we do not know which - Passover, since Scripture opens with it, or Sukkot, since its commandments are many (Rashi: sukkah, lulav, willow, water libation) - [that objection is not decisive]. Rather: we derive separation of seven for one day from separation of seven for one day, not separation of seven for seven from seven for one.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Challenge: say Shemini [Atzeret], which is seven for one day. Answer: we derive a matter with no sanctity preceding it from one with no sanctity preceding it, not a matter preceded by sanctity.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Gemara
independentSourceFlow.move: Challenge: is it not a kal va-chomer? If a matter without preceding sanctity requires separation, all the more so one with preceding sanctity.

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Rav Mesharshiyya
independentSourceFlow.move: 'hazeh' (this) is written - [meaning] 'kazeh' (like this): only a case like the milu'im. (Raw reads 'לא הזה כתיב כזה'; Rashi: 'this' is written, 'like this' - only what matches its pattern.)

independentSourceFlow.speaker: Rav Ashi
independentSourceFlow.move: Is there anything whose primary Festival does not require separation while its subsidiary does? And even according to the one who says Shemini is a Festival in its own right, that applies regarding 'PZR' ... - sentence breaks off; the mnemonic ('KShB') and the contrast ('but regarding compensation...') continue on 3a.

Open at the end of 2b: Rav Ashi's qualification of the independent-Festival view is incomplete (MID_SENTENCE). The next challenge (Atzeret/Shavuot) and R. Abba's answer are on 3a and are not reached here.

defects.currentClaim: Two alternative 'tzivah' candidates are disqualified: Yom Kippur's 'tzivah' follows the service instead of preceding it (post-facto cannot link to pre-facto), and the offerings passage uses 'tzavoto' which is a different verb form than 'tzivah.'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 2-4 and 6 state a choice among competing candidates ('danin X ve-ein danin Y'), and lines 9-11 (next sugya) make explicit that this is a preference for the more similar candidate, not an absolute bar: where nothing more similar exists, even different words are paired. The field's '(post-facto cannot link to pre-facto)' states an absolute rule the source does not state.
defects.proposedReplacement: Two alternative candidates are set aside: Yom Kippur's 'tzivah' is recorded after the service, so the pre-performance 'tzivah' of the milu'im is paired with the pre-performance 'tzivah' of the heifer instead; and the offerings verse uses 'tzavoto', a different form, while the Gemara pairs 'tzivah' with 'tzivah'.

defects.currentClaim: The Gemara has established that 'tzivah' in the milu'im verse links to the parah adumah. But why not link it instead to 'tzivah' in the Yom Kippur passage (Leviticus 16:34), and derive only the Yom Kippur seven-day rule? Answer: that 'tzivah' appears after the Yom Kippur service was performed, while the milu'im 'tzivah' appears before. A gezerah shavah must connect functionally parallel contexts. Similarly, the offerings passage uses 'tzavoto' (a different conjugation), which cannot pair with 'tzivah.'
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 2-4 and 6 state a choice among competing candidates ('danin X ve-ein danin Y'), and lines 9-11 (next sugya) make explicit that this is a preference for the more similar candidate, not an absolute bar: where nothing more similar exists, even different words are paired. 'A gezerah shavah must connect functionally parallel contexts' and 'cannot pair' are absolute claims not made on the page.
defects.proposedReplacement: Continuing from 2a, where the milu'im 'tzivah' was paired with the 'tzivah' of the red heifer, the Gemara asks: why not pair it instead with the 'tzivah' of the Yom Kippur passage ('and he did as the Lord commanded Moses', Leviticus 16:34), so that the whole verse speaks of Yom Kippur? Answer: we derive a 'tzivah' stated before the act from a 'tzivah' stated before the act, and do not derive a 'tzivah' recorded after the act from one stated before it. It then asks: why not pair it with 'tzavoto' of the offerings verse ('on the day he commanded the children of Israel')? Answer: we derive 'tzivah' from 'tzivah', not 'tzavoto' from 'tzivah'.

defects.currentClaim: The before/after distinction seems subtle. Why does the position of 'tzivah' relative to the service matter for a gezerah shavah?
defects.sourceSupports: The sugya's lines state which pairing is preferred but give no reason why the position of the command matters; the hint asks a question its own lines do not answer.
defects.proposedReplacement: Why does the Gemara pair the milu'im 'tzivah' with the heifer's 'tzivah' rather than with the 'tzivah' of the Yom Kippur passage or the 'tzavoto' of the offerings verse?

defects.currentClaim: The Torah mentions 'tzivah' near both Yom Kippur and offerings. Why can't we derive the separation rule from those contexts instead?
defects.sourceSupports: Line 5 quotes 'b'yom tzavoto' - the offerings verse does not use the word 'tzivah' but the form 'tzavoto'.
defects.proposedReplacement: The Torah uses 'tzivah' in the Yom Kippur passage and the related form 'tzavoto' in the offerings verse. Why isn't the separation rule derived from either of those instead?

defects.currentClaim: Shemini Atzeret looks like the perfect candidate: seven days of preparation (Sukkot) for one culminating day of service. The Gemara excludes it on the grounds that Yom Kippur and the milu'im were both preceded by ordinary, unconsecrated days. Shemini Atzeret is preceded by seven holy days of Sukkot - a fundamentally different situation. A kal va-chomer is then proposed: if a less-sanctified lead-up still requires separation, surely a more-sanctified one does too. Rav Mesharshiyya shuts this down: the verse says 'like this day' - exactly as the milu'im, no more. Rav Ashi adds a practical clincher: Sukkot itself (the primary Festival) requires no separation, so its appendage certainly cannot be stricter.
defects.sourceSupports: Line 28: Rav Ashi's argument is a logical one (primary vs. secondary), not a 'practical' one.
defects.proposedReplacement: Shemini Atzeret looks like the perfect candidate: seven days of separation for one day of service. The Gemara excludes it on the grounds that Yom Kippur and the milu'im were not preceded by holy days, while Shemini Atzeret is preceded by the seven holy days of Sukkot. A kal va-chomer is then proposed: if a case without preceding sanctity requires separation, surely one with preceding sanctity does too. Rav Mesharshiyya answers that the verse writes 'this' ('as he did on this day'), meaning 'like this' - only a case like the milu'im. Rav Ashi adds a further argument: Sukkot itself (the primary Festival) requires no separation, so its appended day cannot require it.

defects.currentClaim: Two independent rejections of the kal va-chomer: Rav Mesharshiya reads the verse's 'kazeh' (like this day), not 'hazeh' (this day), as limiting the rule to a case exactly like the inauguration - more sanctity does not extend it. Separately, Rav Ashi argues the primary Festival itself needs no separation, so its appendage cannot be stricter - the less cannot be stricter than the more.
defects.sourceSupports: Line 27: Rav Mesharshiyya says the verse writes 'הזה' (this), read as 'כזה' (like this). The verse (as quoted on 2a, 'כאשר עשה ביום הזה') says 'hazeh'; the field states the opposite, that the verse's word is 'kazeh' and not 'hazeh'.

Separately, Rav Ashi argues that the primary Festival itself needs no separation, so its appended day cannot require it.

defects.currentClaim: 2b continues the Gemara's analysis of the gezerah shavah that sources the seven-day separation rule. Before accepting that 'tzivah' in the milu'im verse links to the heifer's 'tzivah,' the Gemara systematically disqualifies two other 'tzivah' candidates: the one in the Yom Kippur passage (it appears after the service, not before) and the 'tzavoto' form in the offerings verse (different conjugation). A challenge from Rabbi Yishmael's school - that different verb forms can form a gezerah shavah - is answered by the rule that identical forms take priority when available. The Gemara then narrows 'le-chaper' (to atone) to exclude general offerings (daily, no fixed time), Festivals (three times a year), and a single Festival (raising, then setting aside, the question of whether it would be Passover, with which the Torah opens, or Sukkot, which has the most offerings) - excluded since it is a seven-day service, not a one-day service - and Shemini Atzeret (preceded by sanctified days). A kal va-chomer is proposed and rejected by both Rav Mesharshiyya and Rav Ashi.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 21-22: 'הואיל ומרובה מצותו' - because its commandments are more numerous. Rashi: sukkah, lulav, willow-branch, water libation. The source does not say Sukkot has the most offerings. Lines 8-9: R. Yishmael's school paired two different verbs, not 'different verb forms'. Lines 9-11: the answer is that the more similar candidate takes priority, not 'identical forms'. The summary also omits that the daf ends mid-sentence in Rav Ashi's qualification.
defects.proposedReplacement: 2b continues the Gemara's defense of the gezerah shavah begun on 2a that sources the seven-day separation from the milu'im. The Gemara considers two other candidates for 'tzivah': the 'tzivah' of the Yom Kippur passage, set aside because it is recorded after the service while the milu'im and heifer commands precede it, and the 'tzavoto' of the offerings verse, set aside because we pair 'tzivah' with 'tzivah'. A challenge from the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which paired two different verbs ('returning' and 'coming'), is answered: that applies only where nothing more similar exists. The Gemara then asks whether 'le-chaper' (to atone) might mean the atonement of offerings; after asking how one would know which kohen will serve, and answering that the whole beit av could separate, it excludes offerings because they occur every day and lack a fixed time. Festivals are excluded because they do not occur once a year; a single Festival (Passover, with which Scripture opens, or Sukkot, which has more commandments) is excluded because its separation would be seven for seven days, not seven for one day; and Shemini Atzeret is excluded because holy days precede it. A kal va-chomer is answered by Rav Mesharshiyya ('this' read as 'like this') and by Rav Ashi (the primary Festival needs no separation, so its appended day cannot). The daf ends mid-sentence as Rav Ashi begins to qualify the view that Shemini Atzeret is a Festival in its own right; the qualification continues on 3a.

defects.currentClaim: Verbal analogy: a Talmudic derivation that transfers rules between two passages sharing an identical or near-identical word or phrase. Identical forms take priority over similar ones when both are available.
defects.sourceSupports: Lines 9-11: 'הני מילי היכא דליכא דדמי ליה אבל היכא דאיכא דדמי ליה מדדמי ליה ילפינן' - that applies where there is nothing more similar; where there is something more similar, we learn from the more similar one. The principle is comparative similarity, not 'identical form'.
defects.proposedReplacement: Verbal analogy: a Talmudic derivation that transfers rules between two passages sharing a word or phrase. Where several candidates exist, the more similar one takes priority; a less similar pairing is used only when nothing more similar exists.
